S/N concerns what information stands out, such as specific past results or a pattern across several years. Someone can discuss a pattern with a colleague or study a concrete record alone.

### ### ESFJ and INFJ: two ways to read the same client records

compare_blocks.body:

compare_blocks.body:
Imagine two account managers who both listen carefully and summarise a client’s concerns accurately. Training or familiarity with the client could explain the similarity. The behaviour alone gives you little evidence about E/I or S/N.

Both profiles can be described as using Fe outwardly because both have F and J. The model concerns what people weigh in a decision and how they organise their response to the outside world. Skill with clients depends on the person and the work they have done.

Keep the differences separate. E/I concerns where attention goes, such as engaging with a colleague or reflecting privately. ### ### ESFJ and INFJ: two ways to read the same client records

### ### ESFJ and INFJ: why Fe is dominant in one stack and auxiliary in the other

In type dynamics, Fe is dominant for ESFJ, supported by Si. For INFJ, Ni is dominant and Fe is auxiliary.

That distinction describes the model. Either person could open a meeting by explaining a direction or asking how others are affected. The stack cannot predict their order or skill.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Imagine two account managers who both listen carefully and summarise a client’s concerns accurately. Training or familiarity with the client could explain the similarity. The behaviour alone gives you little evidence about E/I or S/N.

Both profiles can be described as using Fe outwardly because both have F and J. The model concerns what people weigh in a decision and how they organise their response to the outside world. Skill with clients depends on the person and the work they have done.

Keep the differences separate. E/I concerns where attention goes, such as engaging with a colleague or reflecting privately. S/N concerns what information stands out, such as specific past results or a pattern across several years. Someone can discuss a pattern with a colleague or study a concrete record alone.

### ### ESFJ and INFJ: two ways to read the same client records

In a fictional account review, two colleagues have the same usage figures, past contract and new request. They have the same preparation time and neither can quote a price yet. One focus is what the records say about volume, dates and agreed payment terms. Another is whether a recurring change in usage points to a developing need.

The former illustrates Sensing’s focus on concrete details and experience. The latter illustrates Intuition’s focus on connections and possibilities. A trend can prompt a useful question, but it does not establish the client’s reasons. Confirm those separately through the client or authorised material.

Either colleague can review the existing terms and ask what has changed. Experience with the account may make a particular detail stand out. Which document someone opens first tells you little about their type.

### ### ESFJ and INFJ: why Fe is dominant in one stack and auxiliary in the other

ESFJ and INFJ both have J, which points to an outward-facing judging process in the model. F identifies that process as extraverted Feeling (Fe). For ESFJ, E makes the outward-facing process dominant, with introverted Sensing (Si) in support. For INFJ, I makes the inward-facing process dominant. That is introverted Intuition (Ni), with Fe in support.

The two stacks therefore share Fe even though it has a different role. Under the notation used here, they also share introverted Thinking (Ti), which is inferior for ESFJ and tertiary for INFJ. The positions describe the model. They cannot tell you who puts others at ease or which person should lead a meeting.

Their perceiving functions differ: ESFJ has Si and Ne, while INFJ has Ni and Se. In the model, Si relates current information to experience, and Ni brings patterns together into an interpretation. Ne explores possible connections and Se attends to what is observable now. None fixes an order for checking a document or drawing a conclusion.

The Foundation lists Intuition (Ne or Ni) as ESFJ’s tertiary function and Thinking (Te or Ti) as INFJ’s. This article uses Ne and Ti in those positions. See the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj) and the [INFJ profile](/en/personality/infj) for their four preferences.

sections.body_md:
In this fictional account review, both colleagues have the same documents, preparation time and authority. Both can consult teammates or work privately.

Each row illustrates only one of the two differing preferences. Either person can use either approach. The rows show how the preferences differ in scope and cannot identify a type.

| Shared situation | ESFJ: possible emphasis | INFJ: possible emphasis | Preference illustrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Reviewing the same usage report | The recorded quantities and changes in specific categories | Patterns across categories and possible connections between changes | S/N: documented details or patterns and possibilities |
| The client says the budget is still open | The stated amount, approval status and dates that can be confirmed | How that statement might relate to patterns in the client’s requests, with the interpretation still open | S/N: confirmed particulars or possible connections |
| A new request comes up during the meeting | Work through what the same request means by discussing it with those involved | Work through what the same request means in private reflection | E/I: outward engagement or inward reflection. Either person can do both. |
| Both prepare for the same meeting | Direct attention to the same points by talking them through with teammates | Direct attention to the same points by reflecting and making a private note | E/I: direction of attention during preparation |
| Reviewing the same delivery history | The recorded dates and the details of the last change | What several changes have in common and what pattern might explain them | S/N: concrete records or patterns across cases |
| Both read the same comments on response times | What each comment says and the circumstances in which it was made | A recurring theme across comments that may be worth checking with the client | S/N: individual observations or a possible pattern |

Account experience and role affect what someone notices. A person preparing to lead the meeting may focus on different details from a person reviewing the same material for accuracy. That is why a single row cannot be used to classify someone.

sections.body_md:
These fictional scenes illustrate how people can use the same information in different ways. Either type can carry either line of inquiry. Assign proposal work according to experience, authority and what the project needs.

### ### ESFJ and INFJ: drafting a proposal for a major client

In a fictional proposal meeting, two colleagues receive the same usage figures and hear that the client wants longer payment terms. Both can ask for clarification. Neither can make a commitment on the spot.

One line of inquiry documents the requested terms, how they differ from last year and who can approve them. Another examines whether several changes together suggest a shift in the client’s purchasing needs. Either person can work on both questions.

Looking only at last year’s agreement can miss a change in demand. Building a proposal around a plausible pattern can overlook a firm requirement. Treat the pattern as a prompt for a question and confirm the answer before putting it in the proposal.

Write two lists: what the client needs to confirm and what you currently assume. After the meeting, check each assumption against the client’s answer or a record you may use. Mark it confirmed, ruled out or open. The exercise checks the evidence behind the proposal and gives no personality score.

### ### ESFJ and INFJ: an unconfirmed remark at a family dinner

In a fictional example, two relatives working on the same account are at a family dinner. A cousin who works for the client mentions a possible change to its suppliers. Both hear the same remark and neither has authority to use it.

They do not ask the cousin for details or put the remark in the account file. They continue to use approved records and ordinary questions to the authorised client contact. The family conversation does not supply evidence for the proposal.

Later, the client shares an approved update with both colleagues. One can compare the confirmed details with earlier changes and list the requirements that now apply. Another can look for a pattern across those changes and ask what possibilities the update opens. Either colleague can do both using the same authorised information.

Those are two ways to take in information. Professional obligations about what can be collected, used or shared apply equally to either type.

sections.body_md:
Listening closely and remembering what a client said earlier are skills people can develop. The shared F preference alone does not establish them.

Quietness does not imply poor client skills. Neither does speaking with ease establish Extraversion. Preparation and familiarity can shape how someone participates, and both types can contribute in a client meeting.

Checking a requirement and recognising a pattern can both improve a proposal. Each needs evidence. The preferences do not rank which person is more careful or perceptive.

The first action may depend on what information is available or what the role requires. Look at several situations with similar conditions and real choices if you want to reflect on a preference.
